title: Web Development for CS
body:
Web Development for CS covers what happens between typing a [[URL]] and seeing a page, and how to write the code at every stage of it. The course runs the stack in order. It starts on the wire with [[DNS]] and [[HTTP]], moves to the document the browser builds out of the response in [[HTML]], [[CSS]] and the [[DOM]], then to the [[JavaScript]] that manipulates that document, then out to other people's data through [[Fetch]] and [[JSON]], and finally onto a server of its own built from [[Node.js]], [[Express]] and [[MongoDB]]. One question decides most of the material: which machine does this run on. A web application is one program split across two computers that trust each other differently, and almost every confusing behaviour is that split showing through. [[CORS]] is enforced by the browser while the server only states a policy. A [[Query String]] reaches the server and a `#fragment` never leaves the user's machine. Cookies are attached to outgoing requests by the browser with no JavaScript involved. Validation in the [[Client]] is a convenience for the user, and validation on the [[Server Side]] is the only validation an attacker cannot remove. [[Web Interview Prep]] is organised around the same question. ## Topics ### What happens when you open a page Before a single line of application code runs, four things happen. The [[URL]] is parsed into parts, and each part is read by a different machine: ``` https://example.com:443/courses/3612?term=fall#syllabus \___/ \_________/ \_/ \___________/\_______/\_______/ scheme host port path query fragment | | sent to the server never leaves the browser ``` [[DNS]] resolves the host name to an [[IP Address]] over UDP, because a machine is reached by number and named by text. [[IP Address]] covers IPv4 exhaustion, the private and public split, and [[NAT]], which is why a home network shares one public address. The browser opens a connection and sends an [[HTTP]] request. The [[HTTP Verb]] states the intent, and the choice has consequences: GET carries no body and asks for something, POST carries a body and changes something. GET and DELETE are [[Idempotent]], meaning repeating them lands the system in the same state, and POST is not, which is why refreshing after a form submission produces a warning. ``` GET /courses/3612?term=fall HTTP/1.1 request line Host: example.com headers Accept: text/html blank line, then an optional body ``` [[Stateless Protocol]] is the design decision behind everything that follows. The server keeps nothing between requests, so two requests from the same person are unrelated as far as the protocol is concerned, and anything identifying the user has to travel with every request. GET parameters travel in the [[Query String]], which appears in browser history and server logs, so credentials go in a POST body. The [[Client]] and [[Server Side]] split is a trust boundary before it is a location, since the user controls the client completely and can edit or delete any check running there. ### HTML [[HTML]] is markup the browser parses into a tree. It describes what each piece of content is and leaves appearance to CSS. ```html

Web Development for CS

Web development for computer science.

Back to courses
``` An element is an opening tag, content, and a closing tag, and elements nest to form the tree. The [[Anchor Tag]] is what links documents into a web. The [[Image Tag]] causes a second request for the file, and giving it `width` and `height` reserves the space in advance so the layout stops jumping when the image arrives. The [[Form Tag]] is how a page sends data back. Its `action` names the destination and its `method` chooses the verb, which decides whether the values appear in the URL or in the request body: ```html
``` In an [[Input Tag]] the `name` attribute is the key the value arrives under, so an input without one submits nothing. The `required` attribute improves the experience of filling the form in and provides no security, since the request can be sent without ever loading the page. ### CSS and selectors [[CSS]] holds appearance and keeps it out of the markup, so one stylesheet restyles every page that links it. A rule is a selector and a block of declarations: ```css .card h2 { color: navy; margin-bottom: 0.5rem; } ``` [[CSS Selectors]] indexes the seven forms, and learning them once covers both styling and scripting, because `querySelector` takes the same syntax. The [[HTML Selector]] matches by tag name, the [[Class Selector]] matches `class="card"` with a leading dot, and the [[ID Selector]] matches a unique `id` with a leading hash. The [[Descendant Selector]] is the space in the example above, matching an `h2` anywhere inside a `.card`. The [[And Selector]] requires several conditions on one element with no space between them, the [[Attribute Selector]] matches on an attribute's value, and the [[Pseudo Selector]] matches a state such as `:hover`. ### The DOM The [[DOM]] is a [[Tree]] of objects the browser builds from the parsed HTML, living in memory on the user's machine. It is a separate thing from the HTML text: editing the DOM changes the page immediately and leaves the source file untouched. ``` document └── html ├── head └── body └── article ├── h1 ← an Element Node │ └── "Web Development for CS" ← a Text Node └── p ``` An [[Element Node]] is a tag and a [[Text Node]] is the text between tags, which is why [[firstChild]] usually returns the whitespace between two tags, and the first visible element is the node after it. [[Node Object]] covers the properties on a node and [[NodeList Object]] covers what a multi-node query returns, which is array-like and lacks `map` and `filter`, so it needs converting or iterating. [[DOM Algorithm]] is the shape of every script written in this course: select nodes, then modify them. ```js const title = document.querySelector("h1"); // one node, or null const links = document.querySelectorAll("a"); // a NodeList, empty if none match title.textContent = "Web Development"; title.classList.add("highlight"); ``` [[Selecting Nodes]] covers the legacy `getElementBy` family alongside these two, and [[Modifying Documents]] covers `createElement`, `appendChild` and attribute access. Each modification can trigger a [[Reflow]], where the browser recomputes the position of everything on the page, so [[DOM Performance]] is mostly about hoisting queries out of loops and batching writes. [[Virtual DOM]] is how [[React]] avoids the problem, by building a description of the tree, comparing it against the previous description, and touching only what changed. ### Events [[Event Handling]] attaches behaviour to a node with `addEventListener`, which allows several handlers on one node and keeps JavaScript out of the markup. ```js button.addEventListener("click", (e) => { e.preventDefault(); // stop the browser's default action console.log(e.target); // the node that generated the event }); ``` The [[Event Object]] arrives as the handler's argument, carrying `e.target`, plus `preventDefault()` to suppress the default behaviour and `stopPropagation()` to halt the event's journey through the tree. [[Event Propagation]] is that journey. An event travels down from the root to the target, which is the capture phase, then back up through every ancestor, which is the bubble phase, and handlers run on the way up by default. [[Event Delegation]] uses this deliberately: one listener on a parent handles events from every child, including children added to the page after the listener was attached, which replaces attaching a hundred listeners to a hundred rows. [[DOM + Event Handling]] covers the two halves together. ### JavaScript [[JavaScript]] has a small set of primitive types and treats everything else as an object. [[JS Functions]] are themselves objects, so a function can be stored in a variable, passed as an argument and returned from another function, which is what makes the event model possible. ```js function greet(name) { return "hi " + name; } // declaration, hoisted const shout = (name) => greet(name).toUpperCase(); // arrow syntax console.log(shout("evan")); // HI EVAN ``` [[Hoisting]] moves function declarations to the top of their scope, so a declared function can be called above the line defining it, while `let` and `const` bindings cannot be used before theirs. [[Anonymous Function]], [[Nested Function]] and [[Immediately Invoked Function]] cover the other forms a definition takes, and a [[Call Back Function]] is a function passed somewhere to be run later. [[Arrow Syntax]] is shorter and changes the meaning of [[This]], which is otherwise decided at call time by how the function was called. An arrow function has no `this` of its own and takes the enclosing one, which is what makes it useless as a constructor and ideal as a callback. A [[Closure]] is a function together with the variables captured from where it was defined, which is [[Lexical]] scoping: ```js function counter() { let count = 0; // captured, and unreachable from outside return () => ++count; } const next = counter(); next(); // 1 next(); // 2 ``` [[Objects]] covers the three ways to create one, through an [[Object Literal]], an [[Object Constructor]] or [[Constructor Functions]]. [[Array Functions]] covers `forEach`, `find`, `filter`, `reduce`, `map` and `sort`. The ones returning a new array return a [[Shallow copy]], where the array is new and the objects inside it are the originals, so mutating an element of the result mutates the source. [[Vanilla JS]] is the language plus the browser interfaces with no framework underneath. ### Asynchronous JavaScript A network request takes hundreds of milliseconds and the browser has one thread for running page code, so waiting for a response would freeze the page. [[Asynchronous JS]] starts the operation and continues, which means the value is absent on the next line. A [[Promise]] represents that future value in one of three states, pending, fulfilled or rejected. `.then` registers what to do on arrival and returns a promise of its own, which is what makes chaining work. ```js fetch("/api/courses") .then(res => { if (!res.ok) throw new Error(res.status); // a 404 is a successful promise return res.json(); // a second promise }) .then(data => console.log(data.length)) .catch(err => console.error(err)); ``` [[Fetch]] issues the request and returns a promise immediately, and the chained `.json()` is a second promise because the body arrives separately from the headers. A rejected fetch means the request failed to complete, so a 404 arrives as a fulfilled promise and `res.ok` has to be checked explicitly. [[Async Functions]] provide the same machinery in a flatter syntax: ```js async function load() { const res = await fetch("/api/courses"); const data = await res.json(); return data.length; // an async function always returns a promise } ``` [[Parallel Fetches]] uses `Promise.all` when two requests do not depend on each other, which takes the total wait down to the slower of the two, where issuing them in sequence adds the two waits together. The [[Event Loop]] explains the mechanism underneath: the callback is queued and runs once the current stack empties, which is why a long synchronous loop delays every pending callback. ### APIs and data An [[API]] is the contract between two pieces of software, and the [[Frontend]] and [[Backend]] split is the largest one in the degree. [[Web APIs]] covers both senses of the term, a third-party HTTP service and the browser's own built-in interfaces. [[JSON]] is the text format the two ends exchange. It carries data alone, with double-quoted keys, and no functions, dates or `undefined`: ```json { "code": "Web Development for CS", "credits": 3, "topics": ["HTTP", "DOM"] } ``` [[CORS]] restricts a page's JavaScript from reading a response from another origin. The server sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` and the browser decides whether to hand the response to the page, which is why the identical request succeeds from a terminal and fails from a page. [[REST]] and [[REST APIs]] cover the conventions endpoints follow, where the URL names a resource and the verb states the operation, so `GET /courses/3612` and `DELETE /courses/3612` differ only in the verb. ### The server side The [[Server Side]] is the only place secrets, trust and shared state can live, because the client machine holds nothing safely. [[Node.js]] runs JavaScript there, and its event-driven non-blocking model lets one process serve many requests, where [[PHP]] and [[ASP.NET]] park a thread per request and pay for one thread's memory per waiting user. [[Node JS]] and [[Server JS]] are the same subject under other names, and [[Apache]] is the traditional server Node replaces here. [[NPM]] is the registry and the command that installs from it. A [[Module]] is the unit `require` loads and a [[Package]] is the unit npm installs. [[CommonJS]] and [[CommonJS Module]] cover `require` and `module.exports`, where `require` returns whatever the loaded file assigned to `module.exports`. [[Express]] adds routing on top of Node, so a handler is registered per verb and path: ```js const express = require("express"); const app = express(); app.get("/api/courses/:code", (req, resp) => { resp.json({ code: req.params.code }); }); app.listen(3000); ``` [[MME]] is the content type header telling the browser how to interpret the bytes, which is why a JSON response rendered as text was sent with the wrong one. [[Cloud]] covers where the server actually runs, and the [[WebSocket Protocol]] provides the server-initiated push that HTTP has no way to express, because HTTP only ever answers. ### Keeping state on a stateless protocol [[Cookies]] are name and value pairs the server sends in a header, the browser stores per domain, and the browser attaches to every later request to that domain. That mechanism is how a stateless protocol supports a logged-in session. ``` Set-Cookie: session=abc123; HttpOnly; Secure; Max-Age=3600 ``` The [[Cookie Jar]] is the browser's local store, and because it is a file on the user's machine, every cookie arrives back at the server as untrusted input. A [[Session Cookie]] has no expiry and disappears when the browser closes, and a [[Persistent Cookie]] has one and survives a restart. [[HTTP-Only Cookies]] cannot be read by page JavaScript, which is the defence against [[XSS]] stealing a session token. The automatic attachment is also the mechanism [[CSRF]] exploits, since a request forged by another site carries the cookie too. [[Cookies and Browser Storage]] carries the flag-by-flag comparison. ### The stack [[Web Application]] is what all of the above assembles into. The [[MERN Stack]] is [[MongoDB]], [[Express]], [[React]] and [[Node.js]], with [[MERN]] as the same acronym written without the word stack. [[MongoDB]] stores documents and offers no [[JOIN]], so related data is embedded in one document or fetched in a second query. [[React]] builds the interface from components that own state and re-render when it changes, using the [[Virtual DOM]] to work out what to touch. ## Related courses - [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]] supplies the fundamentals this course assumes, in [[Function]], [[Object]], [[Array]], [[Data type]], [[Encapsulation]] and [[Copying]]. [[Shallow copy]] here is the JavaScript version of a problem C++ hits first. - [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] covers the [[Tree]] the [[DOM]] is, and [[Selecting Nodes]] is a traversal of it. - [[OPERATING SYSTEMS]] supplies [[Thread]] and the argument for non-blocking I/O, which Node's event loop implements in userspace. - [[PROGRAMMING PARADIGMS]] uses [[JS Functions]], [[Closure]], [[Arrow Syntax]], [[Array Functions]] and [[React]] as its worked examples of functional features in a mainstream language. - [[INTRODUCTION TO SOFTWARE ENGINEERING]] treats [[API]] design as a [[Coupling and Cohesion]] question, and [[MVC]] and [[Microservices]] as design paradigms. - [[CRYPTOGRAPHY]] is what [[HTTPS]] is made of, including the key exchange, the certificate chain and the cipher protecting the traffic. - [[HUMAN COMPUTER INTERACTION]] covers what the interface built here has to do for a person, where [[Feedback]] has deadlines set by perception and [[Accessibility]] is a property of the markup. - [[Web Interview Prep]] re-cuts this material for interviews, extending each section here in [[HTTP Requests]], [[REST APIs]], [[Cookies and Browser Storage]], [[Modern JavaScript Concepts]] and [[Server-Side Technology]]. --- ## Original lecture notes The web works through a client-server model. When a user enters a URL, the browser ([[Client]]) sends a request to a Domain Name System [[DNS]] to resolve the website's domain name into an [[IP Address]]. The browser then uses this IP to send an [[HTTP]] request to the web server, which processes the request and sends back a response (often [[HTML]], [[CSS]], [[JavaScript]], etc.). The server-side can include dynamic content generation (e.g., using [[PHP]], [[Node.js]]) and databases for data management. The browser renders the response, showing the user the webpage.
